research_question: How do bull and bear markets differ, how long have they lasted, and where did the S&P 500 stand in October 2026?

research_brief.purpose: Explain bull, bear, and correction definitions with sourced history and current data.
research_brief.audience: Readers comparing market-cycle terms seen in the news.
research_brief.data_period: Fidelity data since 1872 (Sept 2026 article); Hartford S&P 500 data since 1928 (2025 paper); FRED S&P 500 closes through 2026-10-21.
research_brief.scope_limitations: Price index only (no dividends); cycle counts vary by study method; no forecasts.

keyword_research.historical_note: Owner draft listed Ubersuggest 12,100 / SD 12 for the primary keyword; reconfirmed 2026-10-26.

sources.title: Bear vs. Bull Market: What's the Difference?
sources.limitations: Method and index not fully described
sources.verification_note: Bear market is a 20% downturn from recent highs; 26 bear and 26 bull markets since 1872; medians 19 months/-33% and 42 months/+87%; ranges 1-113 and 14-98 months (quoted).

sources.title: 10 Things You Should Know About Bear Markets
sources.verification_note: 20% bear and bull thresholds; correction 10%-19.9%; 27 bear and 28 bull markets; 289 vs 988 days; -35%/+112%; 42% and 36% strongest days; 15 recessions; 1990 19.9% drop (quoted).

sources.title: S&P 500 (SP500)
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)
sources.method: Index provider data republished by FRED

statistics.claim: S&P 500 price index up about 13.3% in 2026 through October 21; deepest 2026 drop about 9.1%; 2020 drop 33.9%; 2022 drops 23.6% and 25.4%.
statistics.denominator: Prior closing high or 2025 year-end close
statistics.method: Fin Loom calculation from FRED daily closes

statistics.claim: Fidelity medians: bear 19 months and -33%; bull 42 months and +87%.
Hartford averages: bear 289 days and -35%; bull 988 days and +112%.

claims.statement: A bear market is a 20% downturn from recent highs; 26 bear and 26 bull markets since 1872.
A correction is a drop of 10%-19.9%; 42% of the strongest days occurred during a bear market.
S&P 500 closed at 7,757.17 on October 21, 2026 and 6,845.50 on December 31, 2025.
